a@<B>-a,</B> affixed to words, denotes <I>A person, an agent,</I> or <I>actor,</I> hence, <I>All nouns ending in</I> a <I>are masculine, and make the gen. in</I> an; as from Cum <I>come</I> [<I>thou</I>], cuma <I>a person who comes,</I> or <I>a guest:</I> Swīc <I>deceive</I> [<I>thou</I>], swica <I>a traitor:</I> Worht <I>wrought,</I> wyrhta <I>a workman, wright:</I> Fōregeng <I>foregoing,</I> fōregenga <I>a foregoer:</I> Beād <I>or</I> gebēd <I>a supplication, praying,</I> beāda <I>a person who supplicates</I> or <I>prays:</I> Bytl <I>a beetle</I> or <I>hammer,</I> bytla <I>a hammerer, builder.</I> Some <I>abstract nouns,</I> and words denoting <I>inanimate things,</I> end in -a; and these words, having the same declension as those which signify <I>Persons</I> or <I>actors,</I> are masculine; as Hlīsa, an; <I>m. fame:</I> Tīma, an; <I>m. fame:</I> Līchama, an; <I>m. a body:</I> Steorra, an; <I>m. a star:</I> Gewuna, an; <I>m. a custom, habit.</I>@a,-a,a-

ae@<B>Æ.</B> The short or unaccented Anglo-Saxon <B>æ</B> has a sound like <I>ai</I> in m<I>ai</I>n and f<I>ai</I>ry, as appears from these cognate words :-- Wæl <I>wail,</I> brædan <I>to braid,</I> nægel <I>a nail,</I> dæg, spær, læt, snæce, mæst, æsp, bær, <I>etc.</I> <B>2.</B> The short or unaccented <B>æ</B> stands only (1) before a single consonant; as Stæf, hwæl, dæg: (2) a single consonant followed by <I>e</I> in nouns; Stæfes, stæfe, hwæles, dæges, wæter, fæder, æcer: (3) or before <I>st, sc, fn, ft;</I> Gæst, æsc, hræfn, cræft: (4) before <I>pp, bb, tt, cc, ss;</I> Æppel, cræbba, hæbben, fætte, fættes, wræcca, næsse: (5) before double consonants, arising from the inflection of monosyllabic adjectives :-- Lætne, lætre, lætra, from læt <I>late;</I> hwætne, hwætre, hwætra from hwæt <I>quick.</I> <B>3.</B> In the declension of monosyllabic nouns and adjectives, <B>e</B> is rejected from the short or unaccented <B>æ,</B> and becomes <B>a,</B> when a single consonant, or <I>st, sc,</I> is followed by <I>a, o, u</I> in nouns, and by <I>a, o, u, e</I> in adjectives; as Stæf, <I>pl.</I> stafas, <I>g.</I> stafa, <I>d.</I> stafum; hwæl, <I>pl.</I> hwalas; dæg, <I>pl.</I> dagas. <I>adj.</I> Læt <I>late; g. m. n.</I> lates; <I>d.</I> latum; se lata <I>the late;</I> latost, latemest, <I>latest:</I> Smæl <I>small; g. m. n.</I> smales; <I>d.</I> smalum; se smala <I>the small,</I> etc. See short <I>a</I> in <B>B. 3,</B> p. 1, col. 1. <B>4. æ-,</B> prefixed to words, like <B>a-,</B> often denotes <I>A negative, deteriorating</I> or <I>opposite signification,</I> as <I>From, away, out, without,</I> etc. Like <B>a, ge,</B> etc. <B>æ</B> is sometimes prefixed to <I>perfect tenses and perfect participles</I> and other words without any perceptible alteration in the sense; as Cēled, æ-cēled <I>cooled.</I> <B>5.</B> The Anglo-Saxon Rune for <B>æ</B> is RUNE, which is also put for æsc <I>an ash-tree,</I> the name of the letter. v. æsc.<B>B.</B> The long or accented <B>ǣ</B> has the sound of <I>ea</I> in m<I>ea</I>t, s<I>ea.</I> The <B>ǣ</B> is found in the following words, which are represented by English terms of the same signification, having <I>ea</I> sounded as in <I>deal, fear;</I> Dǣl, fǣr, drǣd, lǣdan, brǣdo, hǣto, hwǣte, hǣþ, hǣðen, clǣne, lǣne, sǣ, ǣr, hǣlan, lǣran, tǣcan, tǣsan, tǣsel, wǣpen, <I>etc.</I> <B>2.</B> The <B>ǣ</B> is known to be long, and therefore accented, when in monosyllables, assuming another syllable in declining, <B>ǣ</B> is found before a single consonant or <I>st, sc,</I> and followed in nouns by <I>a, o, u,</I> and in adjectives by <I>a, o, u,</I> or <I>e;</I> as Blǣda <I>fruits;</I> blǣdum: Dwǣs <I>dull; g. m.</I> dwǣses. The <B>ǣ</B> is often changed into <B>ā</B>; as Stǣnen <I>stony,</I> stān <I>a stone;</I> lǣr, lār <I>lore.</I>@æ

fiscnoth@<B>fisc-noþ.</B> <I>Substitute :</I> <B>fiscnoþ</B> (-naþ), fixnoþ, es; <I>m.</I> <B>I.</B> <I>fishing, the action or practice of taking fish,</I> (1) by persons :-- Heora fixnoðe gelamp micel earfoðnys . . . Wē rǣdað . . . þæt Drihten hēte tuwa āwurpan net on fixnoðe, ǣne ǣr his ðrowunge, and ōðre sīðe æfter his ǣriste . . . Se ǣrra fixnoð getācnode þās andwerdan gelaðunge . . ., and se æftra fixnoð getācnode þā tōwerdan gelaðunge gecorenra manna tō ðām ēcan līfe. On ðām ǣrran fixnoðe wurdon swā fela gelæhte þæt þæt net tōbærst . . . On ðǣm æftran fixnoðe wurdon gelæhte manega fixas, and þæt net swā þeāh āðolode. Hml. Th. ii. 290, 5-21. Lǣrde hē ꝥ hī on fiscnaðe him andlyfene sōhton . . . ; ac seō þeōd þone cræft ne cūþe ðæs fiscnoþes nemne tō ǣlum ānum <I>docuit eos piscando uictum quaerere . . . ; sedpiscandi peritia genti nulla nisi ad anguillas tantum inerat,</I> Bd. 4, 13 ; Sch. 420, 5-11. Petrus gecyrde eft tō his fixnoðe . . . ōðer is þæt man him ðurh fīxnoðe bigleofan tilige, and ōðer þæt man ðurh toll feoh gegadrige, Hml. Th. ii. 288, 17-30. Hē hēt hȳ āweorpan heora net on fixnode. Nap. 22, 32. Far ðē on fiscnoð mid mē, Ap. Th. 12, 6. (2) by other living creatures :-- Geseah hē scealfran . . . ēhtende þǣra fixa . . . þā bebeād hē þām scealfrum ꝥ hī geswicon þæs fixnoðes, Hml. S. 31, 1323. <B>II.</B> <I>a place where there is fishing, a fishing-ground</I> :-- Wǣron twēgen gebrōþra . . . and hæfdon ǣnne fixnoþ on ānum brādum mere . . . ac þǣr wurdon eft æt þām wæterscipe micele gefeoht for þām fixnoþe. Se bisceop . . . ābæd æt Gode ꝥ hē worhte þone wæterscipe tō yrþlande, and ꝥ wæter gewænde of þām fixnoðe, and wæs se mere āwend tō felda, swā ꝥ man erode ealne þone fixnoþ, Nap. 22, 21-28. Hē stōd mid ðām folce swā wið ǣnne fixnoð, ꝥ wæs ān brād mere Genesareð gehāten, 30. Sī ðis mynster fram eallum eorðlicum þeōwdðme freōh . . . , ðæt is on feldum and on lǣsewum, . . . and on sealtum merscum, and on fiscnoðum, C. D. iii. 350, 8. Mid allum ðǣmnytnessum ge on fixnoðum ge on mēdwum, v. 186, 5. III. <I>what is caught, a catch, draught of fishes</I> :-- Cwæð hē : 'Wurp fit UNCERTAIN þīn net, and þē fixnoð (fiscnoð, <I>v.l.</I>) becymð.' . . . Wearp þā ūt his net, and þǣr wearð oninnan ān ormǣte leax, Hml. S. 31, 1273. Ne bærst heora net on ðisum fixnoðe . . .; and þes fixnoð getācnað þā hālgan gelaðunge, ꝥ is eall crīsten folc . . . Se fixnoð æfter his ǣriste getācnode þā gesǣligan Crīstenan . . . þā þā Petrus geseah swylcne fixnoð mid hym, þā feōl hē tō þæs Hǣlendes cneōwum . . . gif@<B>gif.</B> <I>Add: Conj, introducing a conditional clause. The indicative after</I> gif <I>implies the certain occurrence of a circumstance, the reality of a stale, &amp;c., spoken of in the clause, admits the truth of the statement contained in the clause</I>. Gyf þū wylt, þū miht (Mt. 8, 2); <I>here it is implied that the person addressed is actually willing to act</I>. Hū magon wē . . . gif þū his ne meaht ōr āreccan? (Dan. 133); <I>here the inability on the part of the person addressed to give any account of the matter is taken as certain</I>. Gif gē mē lufiad, healdad mīne beboda <I>you do love me, so keep my commandments. The difference between the indicative and subjunctive after</I> gif <I>may be illustrated by the following passages</I> :-- Gif cyning æt mannes hām drincæd and þǣr man lyswæs hwæt gedō. Ll. Th. i. 4, 1-2; <I>here the entertainment of the king is an event sure to take place, so</I> drincæd <I>is indicative; but the wrong-doing is quite uncertain, so</I> gedō <I>is subjunctive. (See also</I> 2, 8-9.) Gif man frīgne mannan ofsleahd, 4, 6; <I>but</I> gif in cyninges tūne man mannan ofsleā, 4, 4: <I>for homicide was a certainty, but that it should take place in a king's town was not so</I>. Cf. <I>too</I> gif frīg man frēum steld, 6, 2, <I>with</I> gif frīg man cyninge stele, 4, 3. <I>Perhaps the different renderings of the same Latin words are intended to mark a</I><I>change in the speaker's mind, token in</I> Mt. 4, 3 si filius Dei es <I>is translated</I> gyf þū Godes sunu sȳ, <I>while in</I> v. 6 <I>the rendering is</I> gyf þū Godes sunu eart. <I>But sometimes the distinction seems not very clearly marked.</I> Cf. <I>with</I> Ll. Th. i. 4, 1-2 (v. supra): Gif mon hafad spere ofer eaxle and hine mon on āsnāsed . . . Gif beforan eāgum āsnāse, 84, 12-14: <I>here</I> on āsnāse (<I>like</I> gedō) <I>might have been expected.</I> Cf. <I>too</I>, gif mec deād nimed, B. 447, <I>with</I> gif mec hilde nime, 452, <I>the reference is to the same peril in each: and</I> gif gē syndon þegnas . . . . An. 344, <I>with</I> gif þū þegn siē . . . , 417, <I>the evidence of thaneship is the same in both cases</I>. Gif ceorl būton wīfes wīsdōme deōflum gelde . . . Gif būtwū deōflum geldad. . . , Ll. Th. i. 40, 4-6. Agif. . . ; gif þū . . . aldres rēce . . . þū sweltan scealt . . . , gif þū wyrnest, Gen. 2654 - 2660: <I>here the certainty seems to belong rather to</I> rēce <I>than to</I> wyrnest. <I>See also in</I> Mk. L. 12, 19: gef brōder deād siē l bid (<I>mortuus fuerit</I>). <B>I.</B> the conditional clause in the indic., and (l) present or future tense, (a) the principal clause present or future <I>if, when</I> :-- Ealle þās ic sylle þē, gyf þū feallende tō mē geeādmētst (<I>adora-veris</I>). Mt. 4, 9: Bl. H. 27, 18 : 13, 9: Jul. 169 : Jn. 8, 52 : 14, 14 : Gen. 2315: Exod. 560: 13, 1182. Gyf hē þē gehȳrd (<I>audierit</I>), þū gestadelast þīnne brōdor, Mt. 18, 15. Gif wē willaþ nū on Drihten ge-lȳfan, þonne beō wē sittende be þǣm wege, Bl. H. 23, 7: Bt. 3, 4; F. 6, 16: Sat. 251: Gen. 559: 2521: Sch. 35. Him (<I>the blind man</I>) bid mycel daru, gif hē hit geseōn ne mæg, Bl. H. 21, 8. Þū ne bist unscyl-dig wid mē, gif þū on īdelnesse cȳst mīnne noman (cf. <I>nec habebit in-sontem Dominus eum, qui assumpserit nomen Domini frustra</I>, Ex. 20, 7) Ll. Th. i. 44, 8: Cri. 1310 : Mōd. 45 : An. 1570 : 1614. Meaht þū Adame gestȳran, gif þū his willan hæfst, Gen. 569: 570: 578: Cri. 78i: B. 1185 : 1822. Gyf gē þā lufiad (<I>diligatis</I>) þe eōw lufiad (<I>diligunt</I>), hwylce mēde habbad gē?, Mt. 5, 46: 47. Hū mæg ǣnig man ryht-wīslīce ācsigan, gif hē nān grot rihtwīsnesse on him næfþ?, Bt. 35, I; F. 156, 6 : 7, 2 ; F. 18, 6: Met. 22, 46. Gief (gif, <I>v. l.</I>) wē donne habbad suā micle sorge . . . , donne hæbbe wē bēgen fēt gescōde untǣllīce, Past. 45, 10. Gif (gife, L.) þīn eāge bid mānfull, eal þīn līchama byd þȳsterfull, Mt. 6, 23: Lk. 12, 45. (a α) where the condition depends upon what is implied in the principal clause :-- Þū gehǣtst. . . ēce līf, gif wē sōd and ryht symle gelǣstad <I>thy promise is that we shall have eternal life, if we ever do truth and right</I>, Hy. 7, 75. (b) the principal clause im-perative :-- Gyf þīn brōdor syngad (syngige, R. L. , <I>peccauerit</I>) wid þē, gā and stȳr him. Mt. 18, 15 : 16 : 17. Gif gē Abrahames beam synt, wyrcead Abrahames weorc, Jn. 8, 39. Gif gē mē lufiad (<I>diligitis</I>), healdad mīne beboda, 14, 15. Gif man wid cyninges msegdenman geliged, .UNCERTAIN. scillinga gebēte, Ll. Th. i. 6, 4 (<I>and often</I>), (c) where the clause on which the condition depends is dependent :-- Ðæt wē gedōn, swā wē eāde magon, gif wē dā stilnesse habbad, Past. 7, 9. (d) the principal clause past :-- Gif hī nu gōde sint, þonne wǣron hī swā gesceapene, Bt. 14, 2 ; F. 42, 36. (2) in the past tense, and the principal clause (pres. or fut.) indic, or imper. :-- Gif ic þwōh eōwre fēt, gē sceolon þweān eōwer ǣlc ōdres fēt, Jn. 13, 14. Gif þū . . . gesealdest, hit is riht. Srt. 7, 4-5. <B>II.</B> the conditional clause in the subjunctive, and (l) present tense, (a) the principal clause imperative :-- Gif þū siē Godes sunu, cweþ ꝥ þā stānas tō hlāfum geweorþan, Bl. H. 27, 7:12. Be don gif mon ōdres godsunu ofsleā. Gif hwā ōdres sunu sleā . . . , siē siō mǣgbōt and siō manbōt gelīc, Ll. Th. i. 150, 11-14 (<I>and often</I>). Gif þē þæt gelimpe . . . , þonne þū gecȳd, El. 441. Gib Eādwald leng lifige . . . geselle et dēm londe .x. dūsenda, C. D. i. 256, 5. Gief hwā hit ābrecan wille, hæbbe him wid God gemǣne, iii. 168, 25: 180, 22. (b) the principal clause indic. (pres. or fut.) :-- Gif hwylc gōd man from gōde gewīte, donne ne bid hē þe mā fullīce gōd. Bt. 37, 3; F. 190, 28. Gif hit eōwer ǣnig mæge gewendan, . . . sōna hiē him þe lādran beōd, Gen. 427. (c) where the clause on which the condition depends is dependent, and (α) present :-- Āhycgan, þæt wē on Adame, gif wē mægen, . . . andan gebētan, Gen. 398. (β) past with pres. or fut. sense :-- God hæfde getiohhod . . . gif hī done frȳdōm teala gehealdon, ꝥ hē hī wolde weorþian, Bt. 41, 3; F. 248, 10. (d) where the condition does not apply directly to the principal clause, but must be inferred :-- Gif þū dā nȳdþearfe witan wille, þonne is þæt mete and drync and clāþas <I>if you want to know what is needful</I>, [<I>I will tell you;</I>] <I>it is meat and drink and clothes</I>, Bt. 14, l; F. 42, 4. Gif God wǣre eōwre fæder, witodlīce gē lufedon mē <I>si Deus pater uester essei, diligeretis utique me</I>, Jn. 8, 42. had@<B>-hād</B> <I>a suffix forming abstract nouns,</I> e. g. bisceop-, cild-, man-, wer-hid, etc. In the oldest English it is found combined only with nouns, while in the later stages of the language, as in <I>O. Sax. O. Frs. O. H. Ger.</I> words are formed with it from adjectives. An early instance occurs in the Land MS. of the Chronicle 'druncenhed,' 1070; Erl. 209, 35. In later English it takes two forms, -hode, -hede; in modern times, -hood, -head. [<I>O. Sax.</I> hēd : <I>O. Frs.</I> -hēd,-hēde, -heid : <I>O. H. Ger.</I> -heit, -heiti : <I>Ger.</I> -heit : <I>Dan.</I> -hed.] v. hād.@-had,had

lahslit@<B>lah-slit;</B> <I>n</I>[?]; -sliht, -slite, es; <I>m;</I> -slitt, e: <I>f.</I> According to its component parts the word means <I>a breach or violation of the law;</I> in the Laws however it is applied to <I>the fuse payable for the breach,</I> and is used only with reference to the Danes, the corresponding term among the English being <I>wīte</I> :-- Beō se wið ðone cyningc hundtwelftig scill. scyldig on Engla lage ... and on Dena lage lahslites scyldig, L. C. S. 15; Th. i. 384, 15. Gebēte ðæt be ðæm ðe seō dǣd sȳ swā be wīte swā be lahslitte [lahslite, MS. B.] <I>let him make'bot' for that according to what the deed is, either by 'wite' [if English] or by 'lahslit' [if Danish],</I> L. E. G. 3; Th. i. 168, 6. Gif preōst fulluhtes forwyrne ðam ðe ðæs þearf sȳ, gylde wīte mid Englum and mid Denum lahslit, ðæt is twelf ōran, 10-13. Gylde swā wīfe swā lahslitte [lahslite, MS. B], 2; Th. i. 168, 3. Gylde lahslitte inne on Deone lage and wīte mid Englum, 7; Th. i. 172, 3. Lahslite, 8; Th. i. 172, 7. Lahslit, 9; Th. i. 172, 11. Ðonne gilde hē lahsliht, L. N. P. L. 51: 52: 53; Th. ii. 298, 9: 12: 15. The word is continued in the Laws of William the Conqueror :-- In Danelahe erit iii forisfactura de suo <I>laslite</I> [<I>laxlite</I> in French], Th. i. 483, 24. In Th. i. 168, note a, a passage is quoted from old Swedish law in which 'lagsliht' occurs. See also Grmm. R. A. 623: Steenstrup's Normannerne, iv. 264 sqq.@lah-slit

senatus@<B>senatus</B> <I>the senate, senators.</I> The treatment of this word in the translation of Orosius is somewhat exceptional. The Latin form <I>senatus</I> occurs in the nom. and acc. , but in the former <I>senatas, senatum,</I> and in the latter <I>senatum, senatos</I> are also used; in the gen. <I>senatuses, senatusa</I> are found, and in the dat. <I>senatum;</I> in every case but one (?) the word is plural. The Latin <I>senator</I> is also used, though the word <I>witan</I> is generally employed to denote the senators :-- Sceoldon ealle hiera senatus (senatas, Bos. 43, 5) cuman . . . sceoldon hiera senatus (-as) rīdan, . Ors. 2, 4; Swt. 70, 24, 28. Ealle heora senatus <I>senatores,</I> 4, 9 ; Swt. 190, 19. Ealle ða senatus <I>omnis senatus,</I> 5, 12; Swt. 240, 13. Ðā wolde ān (woldan, Bos. 70, 36) senatus hiene āweorpan . . . Ðā bæd his fæder ðæt ða senatum (<I>altered to</I> senatus <I>in other MSS.</I>) forgeāfen ðæm suna ðone gylt, 3, 10 ; Swt. 140, 14-16. Se consul bæd ðætte senatus him fultum sealdon, 4, 9; Swt. 192, 22. Ða senatus him hæfden ða dǣd forboden . . . Ne mehten ða senatus nǣnne consul under him findan, 4, 10; Swt. 196, 7 -- 10. Būton his āgnum fultume and būton ðara senatuses, 5, 12; Swt. 242, 1. Hē forneāh nānne ðara senatusa ne lēt cucne <I>plurimos senatorum ad mortem coegit,</I> 6, 2 ; Swt. 256, 1. (Cf. Ðara senatornm xxxv <I>triginta quinque senatores,</I> 6, 4; Swt. 260, 23 : 6, 14; Swt. 268, 28. ) Hē sende tō ðǣm senatum ðæt hē ðæt irre gesette wið hiē, 4, 11; Swt. 206, 26: 2, 6; Swt. 88, 12. thorp@<B>þorp,</B> þrop, es; <I>m.</I> Perhaps the idea at first connected with the words is that of an assemblage, cf. the use in Icelandic: Maðr heitir einnhverr ... þorp ef þrīr ero, Skāldskaparmāl; þyrpast <I>to crowd, throng:</I> þyrping <I>a crowd:</I> later the word may have been used of the assemblage of workers on an estate, and also of the estate on which they worked; all three ideas seem to be implied in one or other of the following glosses :-- Tuun, þrop, ðrop <I>conpetum,</I> Txts. 53, 557: Wrt. Voc. ii. 15, 7. <I>Compitum</I> i. <I>villa vel</I> þingstōw <I>vel</I> þrop, 132, 56. Þrop <I>fundus,</I> i. 37, 51. The idea of an estate belongs to the word in Gothic: Þaurp ni gastaistald <I>άγρόν oυtonos;κ έκτησάμην,</I> Neh. 5, 16. In the end the meaning came to be <I>hamlet, village,</I> in which sense it remained for some time in English, e.g.: Ic Ædgar gife freodom Sce Petres mynstre Medeshamstede of kyng and of biscop, and ealle þa þorpes þe ðærto lin: ðæt is, Æstfeld and Dodesthorp and Ege and Pastun, Chr. 963; Erl. 121, 40. He com to Bethfage, swo hatte þe prop, O. E. Homl. ii. 89, 13. Ther stod a throp ... in which that poure folk hadden her bestes and her herbergage, Chauc. Cl. T. 199. Thorp, litell towne or thoroughfare <I>oppidum,</I> Prompt. Parv. 492. The word is now obsolete, but it remains in a great many local names, either alone or in composition; though, as such names are found mostly in those parts of England which were affected by the Danes, its occurrence in them may be due rather to Scandinavian than to English influence. v. Leo, Anglo-Saxon Names of Places, p. 43 sqq.; Taylor's words and Places, s.v. [<I>Goth.</I> þaurp: <I>O. Frs.</I> thorp, therp: <I>O. L. Ger.</I> thorp, tharp: <I>Du.</I> dorp: <I>O. H. Ger.</I> dorf <I>villa, vicus, praedium, oppidum, municipium: Icel.</I> þorp <I>a hamlet, village.</I>]@þorp

triumpha@<B>triumpha,</B> an; <I>m. A triumph, the entry into Rome of a victorious general.</I> The following explanation of the term was inserted by Alfred in his translation of Orosius :-- Ðæt hiē triumphan hēton, ðæt wæs ðonne hiē hwelc folc mid gefeohte ofercumen hæfdon, ðonne wæs heora þeāw ðæt sceoldon ealle hiera senātus cuman ongeān heora consulas æfter ðæm gefeohte, siex mīla from ðære byrig, mid crætwǣne, mid golde and mid gimstānum gefrætwedum, and hiē sceoldon bringan feōwetfētes twā hwīt. Ðonne hiē hāmweard fōran, ðonne sceoldon hiera senātus rīdan on cræt-wǣnum wiðæftan ðǣm consulum, and ða menn beforan him drīfan gebundene ðe ðǣr gefongene wǣron, ðæt heora mǣrþa sceoldon ðȳ þrymlīcran beōn. Ac ðonne hiē hwelc folc būton gefeohte on heora geweald geniēddon, ðonne hiē hāmweard wǣron, ðonne sceolde him man bringan ongeān of ðære byrig crætwǣn, se wæs mid seolfre gegiered, and ǣlces cynnes feōwerfētes feōs ān, hiora consulum tō mǣrþe, Ors. 2, 4; Swt. 70, 22-35. The explanation is called forth by the passage: Heora an consul forsōc ðone triumphan, ðe him mon ongeān brohte . . . and sǣde, ðæt hiē hæfden bet gewyrht, ðæt him mon mid heāfe ongeān cōme ðonne mid triumphan, 17-21. Hiō nolde ðæt hiē mon drife beforan ðæm triumphan, 5, 13; Swt. 246, 29. Noldān hiē dōn ðone triumphan beforan hiora consulum, 4, 7; Swt. 182, 1: 4, 10; Swt. 202, 24.@triumpha
